questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) State two values of Logic.

(ii) What is an idea? (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two values of Logic.**
- Logic trains the mind to reason correctly and to tell a valid argument from an invalid one.
- Logic helps us to detect and avoid fallacies, and so to express our thoughts clearly, consistently and in an orderly way.

(Other accepted values: it sharpens critical thinking; it helps us to evaluate other people's arguments; it improves discussion and decision making.)

**(ii) An idea** is the mental representation (image or concept) of a thing in the mind, formed by the first operation of the mind, simple apprehension, without affirming or denying anything. When it is put into words, an idea is expressed as a **term**. Example: the idea of "teacher".
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Differentiate between Truth-Value and Truth-table.

(ii) State any Indicator of Implication. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **truth-value** of a proposition is its property of being true or false: it is one value, T or F, given to one proposition. A **truth-table** is a table that lists all the possible combinations of truth-values of the component propositions and shows the resulting truth-value of the compound proposition (or argument) for each combination.

**(ii)** Indicators of implication (any one): "if ... then", "implies", "provided that", "on condition that", "only if".
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Distinguish between the following:

(i) Obvertend and Obverse.

(ii) Mood and Figure. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **obvertend** is the original proposition on which obversion is performed; the **obverse** is the new proposition obtained: the quality is changed (affirmative to negative or the reverse) and the predicate is replaced by its contradictory term, the quantity and the subject staying the same. Example: obvertend "All teachers are graduates"; obverse "No teachers are non-graduates".

**(ii)** The **mood** of a syllogism is the arrangement of the types of proposition (A, E, I, O) in its three propositions, major premise, minor premise and conclusion, e.g. AAA. The **figure** is fixed by the position of the middle term in the two premises (four figures: middle term subject of the major and predicate of the minor, predicate of both, subject of both, predicate of the major and subject of the minor).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) Define a Dilemma.

(ii) Briefly explain the Fallacy of Appeal to Force. (2x2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A **dilemma** is an argument in which a disjunctive premise offers two alternatives and conditional premises show that each alternative leads to a conclusion, so that the opponent is forced to choose between alternatives that each lead to a result he would rather avoid. Form: If A then B; if C then D; either A or C; therefore either B or D.

**(ii)** The **fallacy of appeal to force** (argumentum ad baculum) is committed when a threat of harm or punishment, instead of evidence, is used to make someone accept a conclusion. Example: "Accept my view or you will lose your job." The threat is irrelevant to the truth of the conclusion.
